quote: and that Jane would perceive the sarcasm
content: The slip in the name is real. Grouping the two findings is defensible. Gilovich, Savitsky and Medvec explain their effect as anchoring on one's own internal state followed by insufficient adjustment (Gilovich, Savitsky & Medvec 1998), and Keysar and Barr explain the illusory transparency of intention as "self-anchoring" on one's own meaning. Two findings that share one mechanism, egocentric anchoring on private knowledge, can reasonably be taught under one name. The essay itself calls the effect "closely related" to hindsight bias, not identical to anything.

quote: Additional subjects who overheard the explanation showed no such bias, expecting listeners to understand in only 56% of cases.
content: The note leaves out the numbers that carry the finding. When the addressee had not understood, speakers believed they had in 46 percent of cases; when the addressee had understood, speakers doubted it in only 12 percent (Keysar & Henly 2002). The illusion is that asymmetry, not the eleven-point average: speakers are blind specifically to their failures. The overhearers also knew the intended meaning, since they heard the explanation, and they did not overestimate. So knowing the meaning is not what inflates confidence; being the one who meant it is. The title is hyperbole, but the effect is the one the essay describes.

quote: The letter, phrased in polite diplomatese, was heard by Hitler as conciliatory—and the tanks rolled.
content: Conceded: the anecdote does not survive the history, and the essay should have left it where Keysar and Barr found it. The documented record gives Hitler every sign that Britain meant to fight and shows him betting that it would not fight effectively. The essay's case rests on the Keysar experiments, which it reports accurately, and the anecdote was decoration borrowed from them. Dropping it costs the argument nothing.
